read.sections.0.text.note: "Sculptures" became "patung" (statues, the everyday word); "tembikar" for pottery as in Lessons 1–6.
read.sections.0.text.back: An exhibition in a museum or a class is made from choices. A curator decides which sources are shown, how to give those sources a date and a credit, and which questions are asked. A good label helps visitors tell apart what is seen from what is guessed. No single object, map or photo can tell the whole history of a region. The National Museum of Cambodia, in Phnom Penh, is one example of this. That museum says that its task is to show, protect and explain Cambodia's cultural treasures. That museum keeps statues, pottery and other objects. That is how one museum explains its own collection. That museum does not speak on behalf of every community in Southeast Asia.
read.sections.0.text.source: A museum or classroom exhibition is made from choices. A curator decides which sources to show, how to date and credit them, and which questions to ask. A good label lets a visitor tell what is seen from what is guessed. No single object, map or photo can tell the whole history of a region. The National Museum of Cambodia, in Phnom Penh, is one example. It says its work is to show, protect and explain Cambodia's cultural treasures. It holds sculptures, pottery and other objects. That is how one museum explains its own collection. It does not speak for every community in Southeast Asia.

read.sections.0.simpler.back: An exhibition is made from choices. A curator chooses the sources that are shown. The curator gives a date and a credit for each source. A good label shows what we see and what we guess. One object cannot tell the story of a whole region. The National Museum of Cambodia is one example of this. That museum says that it shows, protects and explains Cambodia's treasures. That is the story of one museum. That museum does not speak on behalf of everyone.

read.sections.1.text.back: The second picture is a photo of the National Museum of Cambodia, taken on 2 March 2011 by a photographer who uses the name Dtfman. You can see red buildings with tall roofs around a garden. You cannot see the objects inside, or how the exhibition's contents were chosen. The museum's own description gives a different kind of information. That description says that its buildings were put up between 1917 and 1924, and that museum opened in 1920. That description also says what that museum wants to achieve. So one source helps us know what that place looks like. The other source helps us know what, according to that museum, it does. Both sources have limits.
read.sections.1.text.source: The second picture is a photo of the National Museum of Cambodia, taken on 2 March 2011 by a photographer who uses the name Dtfman. You can see red buildings with tall roofs around a garden. You cannot see the objects inside, or how the displays were chosen. The museum's own description gives a different kind of information. It says the buildings went up between 1917 and 1924, and the museum opened in 1920. It also says what the museum aims to do. So one source helps with what the place looks like. The other helps with what the museum says it does. Both sources have limits.

read.sections.2.text.back: UNESCO's Shared Histories (Shared Histories) lessons, made together with teachers and historians from Southeast Asia, help learners look for connections between people and places across this region. Now you can be the curator. Choose two source cards from different places or from different parts of the course. Explain a careful connection: something we can ask about with the help of both sources. Do not make up a meeting or a journey that those sources do not show. Then name what is still not certain, and whose perspective is not yet there. Put a credit under each source so that other people can check it. You can make your panel on paper or out loud. A fair account may say, "This source does not tell us."

My second source is a map of Melaka, made in 1604 by Manuel Godinho de Herédia. Both sources help us ask how people made boats and used ports by the sea. sensitiveNotes.0.back: Some cards touch on hard history: Banda in 1621 (the VOC took over by force), Timor-Leste after 1999, and colonial rule in Melaka. Keep the panels about what each source can and cannot show, and never ask learners to connect a source with their own or their family's experiences of war, of having to leave home, home country, religion or ethnic group. If learners look up the National Museum on the Ministry of Culture's page, check that page first: its "History of the Museum" part currently holds an unrelated text about the S-21 prison, and that text is not for this lesson.

educatorNotes.0.note: "The brief" (Justin's course brief) became "rancangan kursus" (the course plan).
educatorNotes.0.back: Aim: learners plan a short, fair exhibition panel with credits from two sources from different places or lessons. Step for reading evidence: model a connection between two cards without making up a direct voyage (for example the Butuan planks and the 1604 Melaka map help us ask about boats and ports, but neither proves that boat went to Melaka). Rubric, four parts of equal weight: accurate dates and places; two sources credited correctly; a connection supported by evidence; one limit or perspective that is not yet there. Give concrete feedback, not only a score. A panel may be written, drawn on paper or given out loud; the 80 to 120 words in the course plan is only a guide, and the example is shorter.
educatorNotes.0.source: Aim: learners plan a short, fair, credited exhibit panel from two sources in different places or lessons. Evidence move: model a connection between two cards without inventing a direct voyage (for example Butuan planks and the 1604 Melaka map help us ask about boats and ports, but neither proves the boat went to Melaka). Rubric, four equal parts: accurate dates and places; two properly credited sources; a connection the evidence supports; a limit or missing perspective. Give concrete feedback, not a score alone. A panel can be written, drawn on paper or spoken; the brief's 80 to 120 words is a guide, and the example is shorter.

educatorNotes.1.back: Misunderstanding to straighten out: that any two sources from this region prove there was a direct connection between their places. Notes on the sources: the details on the cards repeat what Lessons 2, 3, 4, 9, 10 and 11 say; check them against the final versions of those lessons. The museum's aims and dates (buildings 1917 to 1924, opened 1920) come from Cambodia's Ministry of Culture and Fine Arts. That photo shows the inner courtyard and a few old cannons on display, not objects from inside the museum. The National Museum is an example from one institution, not the voice of every community in Cambodia or Southeast Asia.
educatorNotes.1.source: Misconception to address: that any two sources from the region prove direct contact between their places. Source caveats: the card details repeat what Lessons 2, 3, 4, 9, 10 and 11 say; check them against those lessons' final versions. The museum's aims and dates (buildings 1917 to 1924, opened 1920) come from Cambodia's Ministry of Culture and Fine Arts. The photo shows the courtyard and a few old cannons on display, not any object from inside. The National Museum is one institution's example, not the voice of every Cambodian or Southeast Asian community.
